id: The Zebra Goes Wild Where the Sidewalk Ends

prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

I Neon stripes tighten my wall where my crayon landlord hangs from a bent nail. My black father sits crooked in the kitchen drunk on Jesus’ blood turned to cheap wine. In his tremor he curses the landlord who grins from inside the rent book. My father’s eyes are bolls of cotton. He sits upon the landlord’s operating table, the needle of the nation sucking his soul. II Chains of light race over my stricken city. Glittering web spun by the white widow spider. I see this wild arena where we are harnessed by alien electric shadows. Even when the sun washes the debris I will recall my landlord hanging in my room and my father moaning in Jesus’ tomb. In America all zebras are in the zoo. I hear the piston bark and ibm spark: let us program rabies. the madness is foaming now. No wild zebras roam the American plain. The mad dogs are running. The African zebra is gone into the dust. I see the shadow thieves coming and my father on the specimen table.

Please expand the following bullet points into a complete, well-structured text:

- The landlord symbolizes a broader system that profits from and exerts control over the family’s suffering.

prompts.L4:
Please expand the following two-sentence summary into a complete text:

Through surreal, racially charged imagery of landlords, machinery, religion, and captivity, the speaker depicts Black urban life as exploited by economic, technological, and national power. The father’s spiritual and physical destruction, alongside the vanished wild zebra, reveals America’s dehumanizing confinement of Black people and warns of the violence produced by systemic oppression.
prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Neon, Jesus, Chains

outputs.L1:
**I**

Neon stripes tighten around my wall, where my crayon landlord hangs from a bent nail. My Black father sits crooked in the kitchen, drunk on Jesus’ blood turned to cheap wine. In his tremor, he curses the landlord who grins from inside the rent book. My father’s eyes are bolls of cotton. He sits upon the landlord’s operating table, the needle of the nation sucking out his soul.

**II**

Chains of light race across my stricken city—a glittering web spun by the white widow spider. I see this wild arena, where we are harnessed by alien electric shadows. Even when the sun washes the debris, I will recall my landlord hanging in my room and my father moaning in Jesus’ tomb.

In America, all zebras are in the zoo. I hear the piston bark and IBM spark: Let us program rabies. The madness is foaming now. No wild zebras roam the American plain. The mad dogs are running. The African zebra has vanished into the dust. I see the shadow thieves coming, and my father on the specimen table.
outputs.L2:
**I**

Bands of neon constrict my room, while the landlord I drew in crayon dangles from a warped nail. In the kitchen, my Black father slumps unevenly, intoxicated by Christ’s blood reduced to bargain wine. Shaking, he condemns the landlord whose smile peers out from the rent ledger. His eyes resemble bursting cotton pods. He lies on the landlord’s surgical table as the country’s syringe drains away his spirit.

**II**

Bright shackles streak across my wounded city—a shining net woven by a white widow. Before me is a savage ring in which foreign electrical silhouettes keep us strapped down. Even after sunlight rinses the wreckage, I will remember the landlord suspended in my bedroom and my father lamenting inside Christ’s grave.

America keeps every zebra behind zoo bars. Pistons snarl and IBM machines flash, announcing: let us encode rabies. Insanity has already begun to froth. No untamed zebras cross the nation’s plains. Rabid dogs are loose. The African zebra has disappeared into dust. I watch the shadowy robbers approach while my father lies on the laboratory examination table.
outputs.L3:
The speaker portrays a Black father whose life is constrained by several overlapping forces: poverty, alcoholism, religion, and an exploitative landlord. Rather than presenting his suffering as the result of individual failure, the speaker shows how these pressures reinforce one another and leave him with little possibility of escape. The landlord, in particular, represents more than a single abusive property owner. He symbolizes a broader social and economic system that profits from the family’s hardship while maintaining power over their living conditions and choices.

This systemic exploitation is intensified through disturbing medical imagery. References to needles, operating tables, and specimen tables suggest that Black people are treated as objects to be examined, drained, and used rather than as human beings. The nation appears almost like a laboratory or hospital in which Black lives are subjected to invasive forms of control. These images evoke both physical violence and a wider process of dehumanization, implying that the country sustains itself by extracting life, labor, and dignity from Black communities.

The urban environment further reinforces this sense of entrapment. The city’s lights, machines, and technologies do not represent progress or freedom; instead, they form an oppressive network of surveillance, control, and programmed violence. The modern city becomes a mechanism that observes, disciplines, and confines its inhabitants. Within this mechanical landscape, violence seems systematic rather than accidental, as though it has been built into the structures governing Black life.

Finally, the image of the vanished African zebra brings together the themes of confinement, displacement, and erasure. Associated with Africa and untamed movement, the zebra symbolizes a freedom that has been removed or made impossible in America. Its disappearance suggests the loss of cultural origins, autonomy, and belonging caused by displacement and racial oppression. Through this symbol, the speaker mourns not only an individual loss of freedom but also the broader historical erasure of Black identity and possibility.
outputs.L4:
The work presents Black urban life through a sequence of surreal and disturbing images involving landlords, machines, religion, and captivity. These images suggest that oppression is not the result of a single individual’s cruelty but of several interconnected systems. Landlords represent economic exploitation and the denial of secure housing, while machinery evokes an impersonal technological order that values productivity and control over human life. Religious and national symbols, rather than offering protection or salvation, appear entangled with the forces that discipline and dehumanize Black people. The city thus becomes a kind of enclosure in which the speaker and his community are watched, used, and prevented from living freely.

The father embodies the personal consequences of this environment. His destruction is both physical and spiritual: systemic oppression damages his body while also eroding his dignity, hope, and sense of self. Through him, the work shows how racism enters the most intimate spaces of family life. The suffering imposed by housing, labor, technology, and institutional power is not abstract; it is inherited, witnessed, and carried across generations. The father’s fate therefore becomes evidence of a broader national failure, exposing the contradiction between America’s promises of freedom and the actual confinement of Black citizens.

The vanished wild zebra deepens this critique. As a creature associated with untamed movement and distinctive identity, the zebra symbolizes a freedom that cannot survive within systems built on captivity and classification. Its disappearance suggests the destruction of vitality, difference, and natural independence. It also parallels the father’s fate: both the human being and the animal are subjected to forces that seek to contain, transform, or erase whatever cannot be controlled.

By combining these images, the work portrays America as a society that turns Black life into property, labor, spectacle, or threat. Its surrealism intensifies reality rather than escaping from it, making systemic violence appear as irrational and nightmarish as it feels to those who endure it. The conclusion is also a warning. When people are continually confined, exploited, and stripped of their humanity, violence becomes a foreseeable consequence of oppression. The work does not present that violence as innate; instead, it locates its origins in the economic, racial, technological, and national structures that repeatedly deny Black people freedom and dignity.
outputs.L5:
Neon flickered above the midnight street, painting the rain in electric blue and wounded pink. Beneath the sign, a mural of Jesus watched over the restless city—his face cracked by years of weather, his eyes still gentle.

People passed carrying invisible chains: regret, hunger, anger, fear. Some wore them like jewelry. Others dragged them behind, listening to every heavy link scrape against the pavement.

A man stopped before the mural. In the neon glow, Jesus seemed almost alive, one hand raised toward the darkness. The man touched the chains around his heart and wondered whether freedom arrived like thunder—or quietly, with forgiveness.

Then the sign went dark.

For a moment, there was only rain, silence, and the faint outline of an open hand.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal two-part poem about Black life in urban America, using images of landlords, alcoholism, Christianity, racial captivity, technology, and zebras in a zoo.
counterfactuals.output:
### I. Rent Is Due in Heaven

The landlord arrives wearing a halo  
stitched from eviction notices,  
his keys clattering like little prisons  
against the dark republic of his thigh.

Upstairs, a bottle preaches itself empty.  
Uncle’s hands tremble beneath the table,  
two exhausted birds refusing to migrate.  
The television baptizes the room in blue—  
Christ walks across the screen in sneakers,  
buffering forever before resurrection.

Outside, police sirens braid the night  
to an ancestor’s iron collar.  
Every phone becomes a small plantation:  
our faces harvested, our voices stored  
in clouds no rain can escape.

Still, Mama sings over the radiator,  
her hymn warm enough to fool December.  
She says God is not the landlord.  
God does not change the locks.  
God is the window we keep breaking open  
with breath.

### II. The Zebra Exhibit

At the city zoo, zebras pace  
inside their barcode bodies,  
black and white sentenced to the same skin,  
while children press their palms to the glass  
as if touching a future behind a screen.

One zebra dreams the fence is a zipper.  
Another chews a map of the subway.  
A third whispers: *Captivity loves a pattern—  
bars, stripes, streets, statistics.*

Downtown, towers blink their silicon eyes.  
Algorithms count us without knowing our names.  
The landlord uploads another moon  
to the rent-payment portal.  
Somewhere, a bottle rolls beneath a pew  
and rings like a church bell.

But we are not only what cages recognize.

We are the hand teaching code to lightning,  
the choir making stairwells holy,  
the laughter that escapes surveillance,  
the impossible animal leaping  
from the city’s concrete ark—

black stripe, white stripe, neither surrendered,  
running past every fence  
the century mistakes for the horizon.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an experimental protest poem in the voice of a child watching his father suffer under racism, poverty, and exploitation; divide it into sections I and II and use disturbing industrial and animal imagery.
counterfactuals.output:
## I. SHIFT

My father leaves before the sun  
has punched its time card.

His boots cough iron.  
His lunch pail rattles  
with one apple,  
two empty hours,  
and a photograph of us  
creased through the mouth.

At the factory gate  
a sign says **MEN**,  
but the foreman says **boy**.

I hear it from the car—  
that small white word  
snapping its chain,  
biting my father’s name  
until it bleeds backward  
through our family.

Inside, machines chew daylight.  
Belts drag black rubber tongues.  
Furnaces open  
like the red throats of slaughtered gods.

My father feeds them his hands.

Each evening  
he returns with sparks  
nesting under his fingernails,  
his spine bent like a crowbar  
someone tried to break.

The landlord circles our building,  
a pale tick growing fat  
on every locked door.

The grocer weighs our hunger  
on a crooked scale.

Police cars prowl the block—  
blue beetles,  
hard-shelled, hungry,  
clicking their lights  
against our windows.

I ask why the world  
keeps calling him dangerous  
when the dangerous things  
have smokestacks, ledgers, guns.

He says, *Eat.*

He gives me the larger half.

The rats behind the stove  
stand up like witnesses.


## II. BREAK

One morning the machine takes  
three fingers from a man  
and does not stop humming.

The foreman writes:  
**CARELESS.**

The machine writes nothing.

My father comes home  
with silence bolted to his jaw.  
His wages are a thin dog  
you can count the ribs of.  
Rent is a butcher  
sharpening the first of the month.

At night he dreams aloud:

*No, sir.*  
*Yes, sir.*  
*I was only—*

His sleep jerks on invisible hooks.

I sit beside him  
and imagine the city as a hog  
wearing a bank for a head,  
its marble teeth grinding  
our school, our street,  
the brown knuckles of every man  
who built the elevator  
but must take the stairs.

They say patience.

Patience is the nail  
through my father’s boot.

They say progress.

Progress is the conveyor belt  
carrying his body  
toward another man’s table.

So I take my red crayon  
and draw the factory split open.

Out spill helmets, clocks,  
contracts, little metal wolves.

Out walks my father,  
taller than the chimney,  
his missing hours returning  
like black birds.

Behind him come the tired—  
mothers with mop-water hands,  
children thin as warning sirens,  
men whose names were fed  
to dogs in uniforms.

We do not whisper.

We become the noise  
the machine was built to swallow.

We become teeth in its gears.

We become the hand  
on the great red switch.

And when they call my father **boy**,  
the whole city answers:

**NO.**
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a dense, hallucinatory Black Arts Movement–style poem that portrays America as an operating table, the city as an electric web, and African Americans as wild creatures confined or erased.
counterfactuals.output:
### **ELECTRIC AUTOPSY**

America lies stainless beneath the lamps,  
a continent strapped flat, ether in its anthem,  
surgeons in white flags rummaging the wound  
for a coin, a ballot, a blackened name.  
The heart monitor chants: **profit—profit—profit—**  
while history, masked, keeps dropping the scalpel.

Outside, the city webs itself in voltage:  
avenues hiss blue venom, tenements spark,  
sirens stitch red lightning through the rain.  
Every window is an insect eye.  
Every wire hums with captured thunder.  
Neon spiders crouch above the corner  
where boys become shadows,  
where shadows become numbers,  
where numbers are erased before morning.

They called us wild—  
then built the cage around the word.  
Panthers behind courthouse glass,  
hawks with clipped paperwork wings,  
wolves photographed only beside the blood,  
black stallions rubbed from the mural  
until the wall itself began kicking.

But listen:

beneath the operating table  
something claws through the sterile floor—  
a drumbeat with teeth,  
a choir of fugitives wearing fire,  
the erased returning as indelible weather.  
The city-web trembles.  
Its electric knots ignite with our names.

America wakes mid-autopsy,  
finds our breath inside its instruments,  
our eyes burning through its anesthesia—  
and all the caged creatures rise,  
not beasts, never beasts,  
but people made monstrous by the mirror,  
breaking the mirror,  
breaking the table,  
carrying the wounded dawn  
between their unshackled hands.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an avant-garde free-verse poem about a drunken Black father, an oppressive white landlord, and a neon-stricken city, incorporating references to Jesus’ blood, cotton, IBM, rabies, mad dogs, and African zebras.
counterfactuals.output:
**Rent Is Due in Electric Blue**

The city flickers  
like a bad idea in a wet socket—  
neon gnawing the windows,  
pink saints, green liquor,  
IBM-blue towers calculating  
how many breaths fit inside a dollar.

My father comes home drunken,  
Black as the hour they refuse to name,  
his coat carrying rain,  
his mouth carrying thunder.

He says the bottle is a door.  
He says the door is a field.  
Behind it, cotton  
keeps whitening under a sun  
that never learned mercy.

Upstairs, the white landlord  
counts locks, counts late fees,  
counts our spoons through the walls.  
His knock has rabies.  
His voice sends mad dogs  
scratching through the plaster:

Pay.  
Pay.  
Pay.

But Father laughs—  
a cracked cathedral laugh—  
and pours his grief into the sink.

“Jesus’ blood,” he says,  
“was not rent money.”

Outside, taxis streak like warnings.  
Billboards breed new hungers.  
The pavement sweats electric scripture.

In the alley, African zebras  
step out of a broken television—  
striped witnesses, impossible and calm—  
their hooves scattering bottle caps,  
their eyes holding savannas  
the city cannot foreclose.

Father kneels beside them,  
not praying, exactly,  
but gathering his name  
from the gutter’s black water.

The landlord keeps knocking.

The neon keeps stuttering.

And somewhere beneath the sirens,  
beneath the cotton, the code,  
the dogs foaming at history’s gate,

a zebra runs—  
black, white, black, white—  
refusing to become  
either cage.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a politically charged prose poem exploring systemic racism and dehumanization in America through surreal metaphors, fragmented syntax, technological language, and recurring images of a landlord, a father, and zoo animals.
counterfactuals.output:
**TERMS OF HABITATION**

America boots in safe mode.

A landlord in a white mask knocks from inside the wall.  
He says *rent* and means blood.  
He says *property* and the deed sprouts teeth.  
Behind him: a ledger, immaculate as a hospital sheet,  
every Black name entered beneath **LOSS**,  
every loss converted into square footage.

My father teaches me how to survive the interface:

Do not run.  
Do not reach.  
Keep your hands where the algorithm can see them.  
Speak softly to the gun.  
Call the error message *sir*.

Outside, the zoo is open all night.

The lion wears a body camera.  
The zebra is stopped for matching a description.  
A gorilla presses his palm to the glass  
and the glass reports suspicious contact.  
Children point. Adults calculate.  
Somewhere, a tranquilizer loads its opinion.

America refreshes.

New headline. Same source code.  
The auction block becomes the precinct,  
becomes the bank, the school district, the app  
that rejects your face because darkness  
is not supported by this version.

My landlord increases the weather.  
Rain costs extra.  
Heat is a premium feature.  
He unscrews the moon from the ceiling  
and invoices us for shadow.

My father coughs in the next room—  
a small engine denied repair,  
a history of red lines mapped through his lungs.  
He says, Son, this country loves a cage  
so long as it can rename the bars:

policy.  
procedure.  
probable cause.  
urban renewal.

At the zoo, the animals dream in human.

The elephant remembers every address  
where a family was extracted.  
The giraffe sees over the wall  
and is charged with surveillance.  
The birds migrate through a no-fly zone,  
their wings flagged by national security.  
The bear learns to smile for the visitors  
because grief is considered aggressive.

SYSTEM ALERT:  
**Your humanity cannot be verified.**  
Select all images containing freedom.

I click the ballot box.  
The burning cross.  
The courthouse steps.  
My father’s hands—empty, raised.  
The landlord’s hands—full, hidden.  
The cage door disguised as a flag.

Incorrect.

America reboots.  
America forgets its password.  
America remembers the whip.

And still my father,  
patched with scar tissue and unpaid hours,  
stands at the window before dawn,  
naming the animals one by one—

Brother.  
Sister.  
Neighbor.  
Child.

The landlord calls this trespassing.

The zoo calls it feeding time.

The machine calls it data.

We call it what it is,  
though the word sparks in the mouth,  
though the walls lean closer to listen:

not accident.  
not glitch.  
not ancient history asleep in a museum—

but architecture, humming;  
a predator made procedural;  
a country teaching its cages  
to recognize us.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
